title: Masquerading: Rename Legitimate Utilities
summary: Renaming legitimate utilities covers two related behaviours: giving a trusted system or administration tool a different file name, and moving or copying that tool into a non-standard directory under a new name. Both target controls that key on the tool's name or its usual path rather than on what the binary does. The binary itself is unchanged, so its embedded version information, original file name field, digital signature and hash still identify it, and the arguments it receives often match the tool's documented usage. Detection therefore depends on behaviour and metadata rather than on file names alone: process creation records that pair a command line with a binary whose version resource names a different product, execution of signed Microsoft or vendor utilities from user profile, temporary or share paths, and copies of administrative tools appearing where they are not expected. Naming rules that simply block a known tool name are easy to defeat and should be replaced with detection of the tool's behaviour, its signer and its expected location together.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker renames a normal, trusted tool so its name gives away nothing. The tool itself still works the same way. Only the label changes. Security rules that look for a tool by name stop seeing it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many monitoring rules watch for specific tool names. Renaming a tool makes those rules blind. Attackers can then use the built-in utility to run their commands without an alert. The same trick hides tools that were copied into unusual folders. This is simple and very common, so you should know it.
howItWorks: The attacker picks a legitimate utility that already exists on the machine.
They copy or move that file and give it an ordinary looking new name.
They may also place it in a different folder to avoid path based rules.
They run it and use its normal features to do their work.
The file is still the real tool, so its behaviour and signature stay the same.
Only name based rules, and sometimes path based rules, are fooled.
beginner.example: Think of a hardware store where the police watch the shelves for a certain brand of lock pick. A thief peels the label off the box and writes tea cups on it. The tool inside is unchanged. The staff watching for the brand name see nothing unusual at all.
takeaways: Detect what a tool does and who signed it, not only its file name.
Execution of signed system utilities from odd folders deserves a look.
Compare the file name on disk with the product name inside the file.

objectives: Describe two ways attackers rename or relocate legitimate utilities.
Explain why name based and path based detections alone are weak.
Identify file metadata fields that still reveal a utility's real identity.
Recognise the differences between this sub-technique and other masquerading behaviours.
Describe a behavioural detection for abuse of a signed administrative tool.
